specStatements.text: Nuclear fission is the splitting of a large and unstable nucleus (eg uranium or plutonium).
Spontaneous fission is rare. Usually, for fission to occur the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron.
The nucleus undergoing fission splits into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size, and emits two or three neutrons plus gamma rays. Energy is released by the fission reaction.
All of the fission products have kinetic energy.
The neutrons may go on to start a chain reaction.
The chain reaction is controlled in a nuclear reactor to control the energy released. The explosion caused by a nuclear weapon is caused by an uncontrolled chain reaction.
Students should be able to draw/interpret diagrams representing nuclear fission and how a chain reaction may occur.
Nuclear fusion is the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus. In this process some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation.

concepts.definition: The splitting of a large and unstable nucleus, for example a uranium or a plutonium nucleus. It is a change to the nucleus itself, not a rearrangement of atoms or electrons.
A nucleus holding a very large number of protons and neutrons that is not stable, such as uranium or plutonium. Only nuclei of this kind undergo fission; small stable nuclei do not.
Fission that happens on its own, without the nucleus being struck by anything. It is rare, which is why fission fuel does not simply split apart by itself while it is in storage.
Usually, for fission to occur the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron. Neutrons are uncharged, so they are not repelled as they approach the nucleus.
What a fission event produces: two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size, together with two or three neutrons and gamma rays.
Energy is released by the fission reaction. It appears as the kinetic energy of the products and as the gamma radiation emitted.

concepts.term: Kinetic energy of the fission products
concepts.definition: All of the fission products have kinetic energy: the two smaller nuclei and the two or three neutrons all move away from the split at speed.
The neutrons released by one fission may go on to be absorbed by other unstable nuclei, causing those nuclei to undergo fission and release further neutrons in turn.
The chain reaction is controlled in a nuclear reactor to control the energy released, so that the rate of fission and the energy output stay steady.
A chain reaction in which the number of fissions grows very rapidly. The explosion caused by a nuclear weapon is caused by an uncontrolled chain reaction.
The joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus.

concepts.term: Mass converted into the energy of radiation
concepts.definition: In fusion some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation, so the heavier nucleus formed has less mass than the two light nuclei had between them.

misconceptions.question: When a large nucleus undergoes fission, what does it break into?
misconceptions.correct: Two smaller nuclei of roughly equal size, together with two or three neutrons and gamma rays.
misconceptions.misconception: The nucleus comes apart into all of its separate protons and neutrons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture the nucleus as a loose bag of particles, so 'splitting' suggests the bag bursting and every particle spilling out.
misconceptions.correction: The nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei. Each of those is still a nucleus holding many protons and neutrons together; only two or three single neutrons are emitted.

misconceptions.question: Which kind of nucleus undergoes fission?
misconceptions.correct: A large and unstable nucleus, such as uranium or plutonium.
misconceptions.misconception: Any nucleus can be split, including small stable ones such as carbon.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The phrase 'splitting the atom' is used loosely in everyday language, so students assume it applies to atoms in general.
misconceptions.correction: Fission is the splitting of a large and unstable nucleus. Small stable nuclei such as carbon do not undergo fission.

misconceptions.question: What usually has to happen before an unstable nucleus undergoes fission?
misconceptions.correct: It must first absorb a neutron.
misconceptions.misconception: The fuel has to be heated to a very high temperature to make its nuclei split.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students have heard that fusion needs extremely high temperatures and transfer that condition across to fission, helped by knowing that a reactor core is hot.
misconceptions.correction: Fission is triggered by the nucleus absorbing a neutron, not by heating. The reactor is hot because fission releases energy, not the other way round.

misconceptions.question: Which particle must the unstable nucleus absorb for fission to occur?
misconceptions.correct: A neutron.
misconceptions.misconception: The nucleus has to absorb a proton, an alpha particle or a gamma ray.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that 'something goes in' but not what. A charged proton or alpha particle feels like a harder hit, so it seems more likely to break the nucleus.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is specific: for fission to occur the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron. Neutrons are uncharged, so they are not repelled by the nucleus.

misconceptions.question: What are the sizes of the two nuclei produced by fission?
misconceptions.correct: They are roughly equal in size.
misconceptions.misconception: Fission chips a tiny fragment off the nucleus, leaving one large nucleus and one very small one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students carry over the picture of alpha decay, where a large nucleus emits a small alpha particle and stays almost the same size.
misconceptions.correction: In fission the nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei that are roughly equal in size. Emitting a small fragment is radioactive decay, not fission.

misconceptions.question: How many neutrons are emitted by a fission event?
misconceptions.correct: Two or three.
misconceptions.misconception: Exactly one neutron comes out, which is just enough to cause the next fission.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students reason that one neutron goes in, so one neutron must come out, and one is all that is needed to keep the process going.
misconceptions.correction: Two or three neutrons are emitted. That is why the reaction can grow: more neutrons come out than went in.

misconceptions.question: Which of the fission products have kinetic energy?
misconceptions.correct: All of them.
misconceptions.misconception: The energy released is carried away only as gamma radiation, so the particles produced are left almost at rest.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Gamma rays are the most obviously 'energetic' item in the list of products, so students assume they carry all of the energy released.
misconceptions.correction: All of the fission products have kinetic energy. Gamma rays are emitted as well, but the nuclei and the neutrons are moving fast too.

misconceptions.question: Do the neutrons emitted in fission have kinetic energy?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. All of the fission products have kinetic energy.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the two smaller nuclei fly apart with kinetic energy; the neutrons are simply released.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams often show the two nuclei being pushed apart, so students give the energy to those and treat the neutrons as passengers.
misconceptions.correction: All of the fission products have kinetic energy, the neutrons included. Fast-moving neutrons are what allows a chain reaction to spread.

misconceptions.question: What carries a chain reaction from one nucleus to the next?
misconceptions.correct: The neutrons released by each fission.
misconceptions.misconception: The gamma rays emitted by one fission are what make the next nucleus split.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Gamma rays are named in the list of products and are known to be penetrating, so students assume they are the active agent.
misconceptions.correction: The neutrons may go on to start a chain reaction. Gamma rays are emitted, but it is the absorbed neutrons that trigger further fission.

misconceptions.question: Why does one fission lead to further fissions?
misconceptions.correct: The neutrons it releases can be absorbed by other unstable nuclei.
misconceptions.misconception: The energy released heats the fuel, and the heat makes the neighbouring nuclei break apart.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students transfer everyday ideas about heat spreading through a material, and they know that reactors get hot.
misconceptions.correction: The chain reaction is spread by neutrons being absorbed, not by heating. Temperature does not decide whether a nucleus undergoes fission.

misconceptions.question: How does the chain reaction in a nuclear reactor differ from that in a nuclear weapon?
misconceptions.correct: In a reactor the chain reaction is controlled; in a weapon it is uncontrolled.
misconceptions.misconception: A chain reaction is explosive by nature and cannot be held at a steady rate, so it must either run away or be shut off entirely — meaning a controlled reactor is not really running one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are described as 'nuclear', and news coverage blurs the difference between a release of radioactive material and a nuclear explosion.
misconceptions.correction: The chain reaction is controlled in a nuclear reactor so that the energy released stays steady. Only the weapon uses an uncontrolled chain reaction.

misconceptions.question: What is the difference between fission and fusion?
misconceptions.correct: Fission splits one large nucleus into two; fusion joins two light nuclei into one.
misconceptions.misconception: The two words mean the same thing, or their meanings are the other way round.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The words look and sound alike, both begin with 'f', and both are met in the same short section of the course.
misconceptions.correction: Fission has the sense of a fissure, a split. Fusion has the sense of fusing, of joining. Fission needs a large unstable nucleus; fusion needs two light ones.

misconceptions.question: Which nuclei take part in fusion?
misconceptions.correct: Two light nuclei.
misconceptions.misconception: Any two nuclei can fuse, including heavy ones such as uranium.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember 'joining nuclei' without the condition on their size, and uranium is the nucleus they have most recently met.
misconceptions.correction: Nuclear fusion is the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus. Heavy nuclei such as uranium are the fuel for fission, not fusion.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the mass in a fusion reaction?
misconceptions.correct: Some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation.
misconceptions.misconception: The total mass cannot change, because mass is always conserved.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Conservation of mass is drilled thoroughly in chemistry, so students apply it to a nuclear change in which some mass is converted into energy.
misconceptions.correction: In fusion some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation, so the heavier nucleus has less mass than the two light nuclei had.

misconceptions.question: In a chain reaction diagram, what should follow one fission that releases three neutrons?
misconceptions.correct: Three further fissions, each releasing neutrons of its own.
misconceptions.misconception: Only one of the released neutrons goes on to cause the next fission, so the diagram is a single chain.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'chain' suggests a line of single links, and drawing one fission after another is simpler than drawing a branching tree.
misconceptions.correction: Each released neutron can cause a further fission, so the diagram branches: one fission, then three, then nine. That growth is what makes the reaction spread.

misconceptions.question: Which part of the atom changes in nuclear fission?
misconceptions.correct: The nucleus. It splits into two smaller nuclei.
misconceptions.misconception: Fission is about the electrons: the atom is split by knocking electrons off it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The only 'splitting' students have met before is ionisation or bond breaking, and both of those really do involve electrons.
misconceptions.correction: Fission is a nuclear change. The nucleus itself splits; the electrons play no part in whether fission happens.

misconceptions.question: What makes a reactor release its energy slowly while a weapon releases it all at once?
misconceptions.correct: Whether the chain reaction is controlled or uncontrolled.
misconceptions.misconception: The difference is the fuel: reactors and weapons use different substances, and that is what sets the rate.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students look for a difference in the material rather than in how the reaction is managed, because materials are the usual explanation in chemistry.
misconceptions.correction: The chain reaction is controlled in a nuclear reactor to control the energy released. The weapon's explosion is caused by an uncontrolled chain reaction.

misconceptions.question: Is fusion the same as two atoms bonding together?
misconceptions.correct: No. Fusion joins two nuclei to form a single heavier nucleus.
misconceptions.misconception: Fusion means atoms joining to make a molecule or a compound.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Joining together' is exactly how chemical bonding is described, so students reach for the chemistry they already know.
misconceptions.correction: Fusion is a nuclear process: the two nuclei themselves merge into one heavier nucleus. Bonding leaves both nuclei completely unchanged.

misconceptions.question: Where does the missing mass go in a fusion reaction?
misconceptions.correct: Some of it is converted into the energy of radiation.
misconceptions.misconception: It leaves as extra particles, such as neutrons thrown out by the new nucleus.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students assume that mass can only be accounted for by more matter, so they invent particles to carry it away.
misconceptions.correction: In this process some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation. The mass is not relocated into other particles; it becomes energy.

misconceptions.question: Are the two nuclei produced by fission stable?
misconceptions.correct: No. They are unstable and are themselves radioactive.
misconceptions.misconception: Once a nucleus has split, the two pieces are stable and give out no further radiation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students assume that splitting solves the instability, so the products must be finished with radioactivity.
misconceptions.correction: The two smaller nuclei are still unstable, which is why spent fuel from a reactor stays radioactive for a long time.

options.text: The joining of two light nuclei into a single heavier nucleus.
options.rationale: This is fusion. Students who treat the two similar-sounding words as interchangeable pick whichever definition they read most recently.

options.text: The breaking of a nucleus into its separate protons and neutrons.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who picture the nucleus as a loose bag of particles, so that splitting it releases every particle separately.

options.text: The splitting of a small, stable nucleus such as a carbon nucleus.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who take 'splitting the atom' to apply to atoms in general and have not registered the condition on the nucleus.

options.text: The splitting of a large, unstable nucleus such as a uranium nucleus.
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition: fission is the splitting of a large and unstable nucleus, eg uranium or plutonium.

mcqs.stem: A power station uses uranium as its fuel. Why can a uranium nucleus undergo fission when a carbon nucleus cannot?

options.text: A carbon nucleus can be split just as easily as a uranium one.
options.rationale: Reflects m02: any nucleus, even small stable carbon, can be split.

options.text: A uranium nucleus is large and unstable, so it can split.
options.rationale: Fission is the splitting of a large and unstable nucleus, eg uranium or plutonium; a small stable nucleus such as carbon does not undergo fission.

options.text: A uranium atom holds more electrons than a carbon atom.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think splitting the atom is about its electrons rather than about a change to the nucleus itself.

options.text: A carbon nucleus can only join to others, never split.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who have swapped fission and fusion, and so file every light nucleus under joining rather than splitting.

mcqs.stem: Spontaneous fission is rare. What must usually happen before a large unstable nucleus undergoes fission?

options.text: The unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron.
options.rationale: The specification states that usually, for fission to occur, the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron.

options.text: The unstable nucleus must be heated to a high temperature.
options.rationale: Students transfer the high-temperature condition needed for fusion, and know that a reactor is hot, so they make heating the trigger.

options.text: The unstable nucleus must first absorb a proton.
options.rationale: Students remember that a particle must be absorbed but not which one, and a charged proton feels like a harder hit than a neutron.

options.text: The unstable nucleus must first absorb a gamma ray.
options.rationale: Gamma rays appear in the list of fission products, so students assume gamma rays are also what sets each fission off.

mcqs.stem: A uranium nucleus absorbs a neutron and undergoes fission. Apart from gamma rays, what does the fission produce?

options.text: Two smaller nuclei of about the same size, and a single extra neutron.
options.rationale: Students reason that one neutron went in, so one comes out, which is just enough to keep a chain going.

options.text: One large nucleus and one very small nucleus, plus a few free neutrons.
options.rationale: This is the picture of alpha decay carried over to fission, where a small fragment is chipped off a nucleus that stays large.

options.text: Two smaller nuclei of roughly equal size, plus two or three neutrons.
options.rationale: The nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size, and emits two or three neutrons plus gamma rays.

options.text: A shower of individual protons and neutrons from the nucleus that split.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who imagine the nucleus bursting and spilling all of its particles rather than splitting into two nuclei.

mcqs.stem: A uranium nucleus undergoes fission. Which statement about the two nuclei it produces is correct?

options.text: They are stable, so no further radiation is ever emitted by them.
options.rationale: Students assume that splitting cures the instability, so the fragments must be finished with radioactivity.

options.text: They are roughly equal in size, and both are smaller than the uranium nucleus.
options.rationale: The nucleus undergoing fission splits into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size.

options.text: One is much larger than the other, and the smaller is a proton.
options.rationale: This is the alpha-decay picture again: a large nucleus that stays large after ejecting one small particle.

options.text: One keeps almost all the mass, and the other is only a tiny fragment.
options.rationale: Reflects m05: fission chips a tiny fragment, leaving one large and one very small nucleus.

mcqs.stem: In a fission event, which of the products are given kinetic energy?

options.text: Only the two smaller nuclei that are formed by the split.
options.rationale: Diagrams show the two nuclei being pushed apart, so students award the energy to those and treat the neutrons as passengers.

options.text: None of them, since the energy is carried off by the gamma rays.
options.rationale: Gamma rays are the most obviously energetic product, so students assume they carry all of the energy released.

options.text: Only the neutrons, which then go on to cause more fission.
options.rationale: Students link kinetic energy to the particle that visibly travels on, and so give the two nuclei none of it.

options.text: All of them, including each of the neutrons that are emitted.
options.rationale: The specification states that all of the fission products have kinetic energy.

mcqs.stem: Why can a single fission event lead to a chain reaction?

options.text: The gamma rays given out are absorbed by other nuclei, making those split too.
options.rationale: Gamma rays are named among the products and are known to be penetrating, so students make them the agent that spreads the reaction.

options.text: The energy released heats the fuel up until the nuclei around it break apart.
options.rationale: Students transfer everyday ideas about heat spreading through a material, and they know that a reactor core is hot.

options.text: The neutrons released are absorbed by other nuclei, making those split too.
options.rationale: The neutrons emitted may go on to start a chain reaction: each absorbed neutron can cause a further fission.

options.text: One neutron comes out, which splits exactly one more nucleus.
options.rationale: Reflects m06: exactly one neutron is released, just enough for the next fission.

mcqs.stem: How does the chain reaction inside a nuclear reactor differ from the one in a nuclear weapon?

options.text: In the reactor it is controlled; in the weapon it is not.
options.rationale: The chain reaction is controlled in a nuclear reactor to control the energy released, whereas the weapon's explosion is caused by an uncontrolled chain reaction.

options.text: The reactor releases energy slowly because it uses a different fuel.
options.rationale: Students look for a difference in the material rather than in how the reaction is managed, as they would in chemistry.

options.text: The reactor splits nuclei, while the weapon works by joining them.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who have swapped fission and fusion and file the more dramatic process under the more exotic word.

options.text: The weapon uses a chain reaction, but the reactor does not use one.
options.rationale: Reflects reworded m11: chain reactions are explosive, so only the weapon runs one.

mcqs.stem: The chain reaction in a nuclear reactor is controlled. What does controlling it achieve?

options.text: It keeps the rate of fission steady, so the energy is released steadily.
options.rationale: The chain reaction is controlled in a nuclear reactor to control the energy released, so the core delivers energy steadily instead of all at once.

options.text: It stops the chain reaction, so that no further fission takes place.
options.rationale: Students read 'controlled' as 'stopped', and then cannot explain how the reactor goes on releasing energy.

options.text: It makes the reaction spread faster, so more energy is given out.
options.rationale: Students equate control with getting the most out of the fuel, which describes the uncontrolled case, not the controlled one.

options.text: It removes the gamma rays produced, so no radiation escapes.
options.rationale: Control is confused with shielding: the word is attached to the radiation hazard rather than to the rate of fission.

mcqs.stem: A student is drawing a chain reaction diagram. One neutron causes a fission that releases three neutrons, and each of those is absorbed by another uranium nucleus. What should the diagram show next?

options.text: One further fission, with the two spare neutrons simply stopping there.
options.rationale: The word 'chain' suggests a single line of links, so students draw one fission after another instead of a branching tree.

options.text: Three further fissions, each of them releasing three more neutrons.
options.rationale: Each absorbed neutron causes a fission that emits two or three neutrons of its own, so the diagram branches: one, then three, then nine.

options.text: Three further fissions, each of them releasing one new neutron.
options.rationale: Students who think one neutron in means one neutron out draw a diagram that never grows, so no chain reaction could build.

options.text: Three bursts of gamma radiation spreading out from the nuclei.
options.rationale: Students who believe gamma rays carry the chain forward draw radiation rather than neutrons as the next step.

options.text: Two heavy nuclei join together to form one lighter nucleus.
options.rationale: Students remember 'joining nuclei' but not the condition that the two nuclei taking part must be light ones.

options.text: A large unstable nucleus splits into two fragments.
options.rationale: This is fission. Students who cannot keep the two words apart pick the process they can describe most confidently.

options.text: Two light nuclei join to form a single heavier nucleus.
options.rationale: Nuclear fusion is the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus.

options.text: Two atoms bond together to make a molecule with one nucleus.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read 'joining' as chemical bonding, which in fact leaves both nuclei entirely unchanged.

mcqs.stem: Two light nuclei fuse to form a heavier nucleus. What may happen to some of their mass?

options.text: It is thrown out of the new nucleus as extra neutrons.
options.rationale: Students assume mass can only be accounted for by more matter, so they invent particles to carry the missing mass away.

options.text: It stays the same, since mass is always conserved.
options.rationale: Conservation of mass is drilled in chemistry, so students apply it to a nuclear change in which mass is converted into energy.

options.text: It is used up in splitting the new nucleus apart.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who have fission in mind and describe the heavier nucleus breaking up again.

options.text: It is converted into the energy of radiation.
options.rationale: In this process some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation.
